lesson.title: Uphill or Downhill: Reading the Direction of an Association
lesson.summary: Learn to identify whether a scatterplot's pattern trends upward, downward, or shows no consistent trend, the first and most basic description of any bivariate relationship.
lesson.body:
An association between two variables simply means that knowing the value of one variable gives you some information about the likely value of the other, a pattern you can often spot directly in a scatterplot. The very first thing a statistician reports about an association is its direction: does the pattern trend upward, downward, or show no consistent trend at all as you move from left to right across the graph?

A positive direction means that as the explanatory variable increases, the response variable tends to increase as well, the point cloud drifts up and to the right. A negative direction means the opposite: as the explanatory variable increases, the response variable tends to decrease, so the cloud drifts down and to the right. When there is no tendency for the response to rise or fall consistently with the explanatory variable, the association has no clear direction, and the points look like a flat or scattered cloud with no visible tilt.

Look back at the study hours and exam score scatterplot: (1, 68), (2, 72), (3, 75), (4, 80), (5, 84), (6, 90). Tracing the points from left to right, the exam scores climb almost every step of the way as hours studied increases. That consistent upward drift is the signature of a positive direction. You do not need to compute anything to state the direction correctly, you only need to trace the pattern with your eye from the smallest x-value to the largest and note whether y is generally rising or falling.

Compare that to a data set tracking a car's age in years against its resale value in dollars. Older cars are consistently worth less than newer ones, so tracing left to right, the value drops as age increases, that is a negative direction, and it is the mirror image of what the study hours example showed. Direction alone already tells you a lot: it is the difference between saying more of this tends to come with more of that, and more of this tends to come with less of that.

Direction is necessary but never sufficient to fully describe an association. Two scatterplots can both show a positive direction while looking completely different, one a tight, obviously linear climb and the other a loose, curving scramble of points that only vaguely trends upward. That is why direction is always reported alongside form and strength, the two ideas covered next, rather than standing alone as a complete description. A written conclusion that only names the direction, without saying anything about how tightly the points follow it, leaves out most of the useful information the scatterplot actually contains.

When you read direction off a real scatterplot, check that the trend holds across the whole range of x-values, not just at one end. A pattern that rises for small x-values and then falls for large x-values does not have a single consistent direction at all, it has a curved form, which is a different property entirely and one you will study soon under form of association.
